text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- There will not be any changes to the extended sick leave period. Prime Minister Goran Persson said at the weekend that it was never meant that sick leave pay would fall by 10 percentage points in the third and fourth week when employers took over paying for those weeks.

- Sweden has not changed its view on the expansion of the European Union or on the question of Nato. Sweden is not any closer to a membership of Nato today compared to before, Minister of Foreign Affairs Lena Hjelm-Wallen told Dagens Nyheter.

- More than half of Swedish voters want to see conservative party leader Carl Bildt as the country's next prime minister, while 25 percent prefer Goran Persson, the current Social Democratic Prime Minister, a survey by pollster Sifo showed. Bildt has become popular while acting as a peace mediator in Bosnia. He is expected to return to Swedish politics this spring.
- Swedish farmers' association LRF calls for the abolishing of taxes on ethyl alcohol to enable the creation of a large ethyl alcohol factory.
- Insurer Skandia could decide to spin-off and list its AFS unit separately within two or three years, chief executive Lars-Eric Petersson said in an interview.

- Swedish furniture company Ikea, with an annual turnover of 40 billion crowns, is fighting against falling profitability. Purchase costs are to be cut by 10 percent and its range of goods will be decreased by 25 percent.
- Products and services worth between 120 and 145 million Swedish crowns will be sold on Internet in Sweden during 1997, a survey by Projector New Media showed.
